newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish budget sets five-point spending plan.
newsitem.headline: Swedish budget sets five-point spending plan.

text.p: A five point spending plan designed to boost employment was the foundation of the Swedish government's supplementary budget released on Tuesday.

The budget proposed spending 5.5 billion crowns in 1997 but stepping this up to 16.3 billion crowns in 1998 as the government battles to bring down unemployment, creating more spaces for students and measures to initiate jobs.
"The government is proposing a five-point programme for work and growth," the government said in a statement.
"The measures now proposed are estimated to lead to unemployment being pressed down to 4.5 percent by the year 2000."
Unemployment in Sweden was running at 8.4 percent in March but the government, facing flagging opinion polls, has pledged to cut this to 4.0 percent by the year 2000.
In its spring budget proposal it forecast unemployment falling to 7.1 percent in 1998 from 8.1 percent in 1996 and to 4.5 percent by 2000, above its target.
The budget proposed spending of 21 billion crowns in 1999 and 23.3 billion in 2000.
The government said state debt was seen at 82.6 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 1997 but slipping to 78.8 percent in 1998 and 75.5 percent in 1999.
"Consolidated gross debt is estimated at the end of 1998 to be equivalent to about 74 percent of GDP which is a reduction of five percentage points from the top level of 1994," the government said.
